newsitem.title: PERU: Peru-Japan crisis summit tests "oriental patience".
newsitem.headline: Peru-Japan crisis summit tests "oriental patience".

text.p: Crisis talks on Saturday between the Peruvian and Japanese heads of state promise to be a test of what Peru's Alberto Fujimori calls "oriental patience" in agreeing on a strategy to handle the hostage siege in Lima.

President Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, has said he would use his "oriental patience" to deal with the roughly 15 Marxist rebels holed up at the Japanese ambassador's home with their 72 VIP hostages.
But when he joins Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Toronto for their first face-to-face talks since the crisis began, Fujimori may find his beligerent tactics have worn thin with Tokyo.

Government officials in Lima and Tokyo have said the summit will fine-tune joint strategy for a peaceful end to the siege which began on Dec. 17 when Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas stormed a cocktail party and seized hundreds of guests, most of whom were freed after a few days.

"With efforts to find a peaceful solution to the hostage situation reaching a critical stage ... it is extremely important that the two leaders exchange views in direct talks," Japanese government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said.
Saturday's meeting followed repeated criticisms from Tokyo that Fujimori was taking risks with the lives of the hostages, among them about two dozen Japanese nationals.
The summit, "is a kind of ear-bending by the Japanese government for what it interprets as poor management of the crisis," said sociologist Fernando Rospigliosi.
Security forces heaped pressure on the Cuban-inspired hostage takers in recent days in an apparent bid to crack their resolve.

Scores of police paraded past the residence to the tune of military marches on Monday, their rifles trained on the building, provoking gunfire from the guerrillas that narrowly missed police making obscene gestures at them.

Instead of unsettling the rebels, the tactics appeared to have unnerved Tokyo. "I'm worrying how it may affect the hostages inside. I'm wondering if I can ask ... the Peruvian government not to go too far," Hashimoto said after the shooting.
The meeting with Fujimori was announced the next day.

Hashimoto, under pressure to improve Tokyo's poor record on crisis handling and a reputation for giving in too easily to hostage takers, has broadly supported Fujimori's tough line of not giving in to MRTA demands for the release of about 400 jailed comrades.
But at the same time, the Japanese leader has tried to rein in Fujimori's more hawkish tendencies.

Many Peruvians feel Fujimori, who has waged an aggressive, and largely successful, offensive against the MRTA and the larger and bloodier Maoist Shining Path guerrillas, would be more inclined to end the standoff by force if foreign nationals were not among the captives.
Fujimori, whose younger brother, Pedro, is among the hostages, has said he will only take such action if one of the captives is harmed.
Saturday's meeting with Hashimoto would allow the two sides to achieve "very close coordination" should such an emergency arise, he told Argentina's CVN network on Thursday.

But Peruvian officials denied Saturday's summit and a meeting last week with Bolivia's President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada, indicated imminent assault. Bolivian Ambassador Jorge Gumucio is the only non-Peruvian or Japanese held captive.

"He will not meet with Hashimoto to apologise for the police attitude, nor is he going to Canada to ask permission (from Japan) to enter the residence (by force)," said a senior government official on condition on anonymity.
Under international law, Peru would need Japan's approval to storm the residence which is deemed Japanese territory.
But with both Japan and Tokyo refusing to give in to the rebels' demands and publicly ruling out paying ransoms for the hostages, a negotiated settlement to the crisis appears a distant prospect.

"It's been a month since it appeared that negotiations between the Peru government and the guerrillas would begin, but we're still stuck outside the doorway," a Japanese Foreign Ministry official said.
